newsitem.title: UK: UK public finances start year on sound footing.
newsitem.headline: UK public finances start year on sound footing.

text.p: Britain repaid a modest amount of national debt in the first month of the new financial year, official figures out on Monday showed, but that was a far better outcome than most economists expected.

The Office for National Statistics said Britain paid back 36 million pounds ($59.03 million) of debt in April. In the same month last year, the public finances were nearly three billion pounds in the red.
Economists had forecast government outgoings would outstrip receipts by about 1.7 billion pounds in April. But the new administration declined to crow about the figures.
The Treasury warned against reading too much into one month's data, particularly at the start of the financial year.
"The PSBR in April...is flattered by a number of special factors including a one-off benefit of asset sales and changes to quarterly VAT payments for big companies," a spokesman said.

The ONS said April's PSBR was cut by a 700 million stg instalment from the Housing Corporation loan book. A final payoff from the sale of Ministry of Defence married quarters also raised 700 million pounds.
Furthermore, privatisation proceeds totalled 172 million stg in April, up from 78 million in April 1996.
Nonetheless, economists said April's public sector borrowing requirement figures were surprisingly good and were aided by both strong tax receipts and low public spending growth.

"An excellent start to the new financial year, with clear evidence that the public finances are benefiting from the strength of (economic) activity," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

Total tax receipts were more than 12 percent higher than in April last year as free-spending consumers boosted the total of value added tax collected to 4.7 billion stg from 3.3 billion a year ago. Income tax receipts also rose, by about 10 percent, from last year.
Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS, said the government had pencilled in receipts growth of six percent this year. "In the first month we've grown at over twice the predicted annual pace," he said.
On the spending side too, restraint has been maintained. Net departmental outlays, totalling just over 21 billion stg last month, were five percent lower than in April last year.
Here too, the robust economy helped, with steadily falling unemployment cutting welfare bills.

"They are a good set of numbers even when you strip out the receipts from the MOD and housing corporation loan book," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch. "It continues the trend we've seen over the last year of growth coming in above forecast and unemployment coming in below forecast and surprisingly good control of departmental spending."

But the Treasury spokesman said there was no way that Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown -- who has promised to keep an iron grip on public spending -- would relax his vigil over the public finances on the strength of one set of figures.
"The Chancellor is determined to see significant further progress before he is confident that public finances are on a sounder long-term footing," the spokesman said.

Loynes said that was entirely sensible. "With the PSBR still uncomfortably high given the stage of the economic cycle, these numbers do not eradicate the need for a fiscal tightening if the public finances are to be returned to balance on a sustainable basis."
Brown will hold a budget within weeks and Loynes expects it to exert a fiscal tightening of around four billion pounds -- enough to push the PSBR down to around 12 billion stg this year.

Figures produced at last November's budget by Brown's predecessor Kenneth Clarke, pencilled in a PSBR of 19.2 billion pounds for the year as a whole. But as the economy enters its sixth year of recovery, Brown is sure to want to undercut that.
